segments: 183 and remained in it for days.
And he strengthened and encouraged the Amir of Tarsus not to fear the Romans;
and he left and came to Aleppo.
And the Romans came out after him from another side,
and reached as far as Mayperqat (Martyropolis),
and took captive and carried off into exile the inhabitants of its territory,
and they burned the villages and departed.
And in the year
346 of the Arabs,
a great swarm of locusts came
and ruined the crops.
And again there was a pestilence among men caused by a choking ailment (quinsy/croup),
even to the extent
that a thief, while he was breaking into the house of one of the rich men in Baghdad,
died in that very breach.
And likewise a judge, when he had dressed in his black garments to go out to the court to judge,
and had put on one of his boots,
fell and died before he put on the other boot.
And in wintertime, a great rain came.
And the Great Sea receded,
and retreated inwards about three hundred cubits,
and many mountains and islands were uncovered that had not been known before.
And after a year, there was a severe earthquake,
and it destroyed many places.
And many were suffocated under the ruins in the mountains of the Daylamites and Qashan.
And the Romans went out as far as Amid, Arzan, and Mayperqat,
and took control of many fortified cities, that is, fortresses,
and killed one thousand five hundred people.
And after a few days, the Romans again marched into the region of Aleppo,
and Sayf al-Dawla encountered them at Daluk.
And the Romans were victorious,
and captured the kinsmen of Sayf al-Dawla and the men of his family,
and slaughtered {OCR: for ܩܲܛܸܠܘ} the majority of the Arab infantrymen,
and none escaped
except a few.
And the Romans also conquered Samosata,
and burned it (or: they burned it?) with fire.
And in the year
to send the tribute money to Baghdad,
there came against him Mu'izz
al-Dawla, the Amir, that is, the general-in-chief of Baghdad.
He, however, fled to Nisibis;
and when Mu'izz al-Dawla pursued him there also,
he fled to Mayperqat.
And he was not able to remain there either,
but fled to Aleppo,
and took refuge with his brother Sayf {OCR: text ܚܝܦ} al-Dawla.
He, then, received him with great love,
and humbled himself before him to such a degree
that even the boots of Nasir al-Dawla, his brother, he with his own hands
